transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-04 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Jordan Lee, Sofia Ramos (Redwood); Mark Chen, Lisa Gomez, Ravi Patel, Nadia Ortiz (Arcadia)

Summary (auto): quick hosted API demo and Q&A around streaming and retry semantics, plus security questions.

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan Lee, account exec at Redwood, and with me is Sofia, our solutions engineer. How are you all doing?
[00:08] Mark: Good, thanks. Excited to see the hosted API. We've been looking at a few providers.
[00:12] Lisa: Yeah thanks, got a short agenda from our side: see the basics, understand latency/cost, and security.
[00:20] Jordan: Perfect. We'll show chat and text gen basics — streaming, params like temperature and max_tokens, and retry behaviour — then leave time for your security questions. Sofia will demo the console briefly.
[00:30] Sofia: Quick note: the demo uses our hosted endpoint and a 2B-ish open model variant for latency examples, not to imply you must use that model.
[00:37] Ravi: Cool. We want to understand expected p99 latency at our hoped QPS and how streaming affects perceived latency.
[00:44] Sofia: Great question. For streaming we send partial token frames over HTTP chunked (or SSE/websockets). So first-byte latency can be lower than full-response latency, because streaming yields the token prefix as it's generated. In our hosted tier typical first-byte for short responses is ~40-120ms on optimized models; full response depends on tokens. These are approximate and vary by model and sequence length.
[01:10] Mark: 40-120ms sounds good. Is that for end-to-end from your API or just server-side generation?
[01:15] Sofia: That's end-to-end including networking from our hosted region to the sample client we used. If you want region-specific numbers we can run the benchmark on your pings.
[01:23] Lisa: What's the tradeoff with batching? We care about cost more than a few ms.
[01:28] Sofia: Right — automatic batching increases throughput and lowers cost per token but adds a small queuing delay. Our optimizer can tune batch windows: aggressive batching for best cost or tighter windows for low-latency SLOs. We also do prefix/KV caching for repeated prompt prefixes to reduce the compute needed.
[01:45] Ravi: You mentioned retry semantics in the agenda — how do you handle idempotency?
[01:50] Sofia: We recommend clients send an idempotency_key per user-turn. For non-streaming requests you can retry with the same key; the server dedups and returns the same result or a consistent error. For streaming, if a connection is dropped we support resume tokens in some SDKs, and otherwise we recommend a new request with the same idempotency key and a flag to return last-complete-token behavior — we can share SDK snippets.
[02:20] Mark: Is there automatic retry with exponential backoff?
[02:23] Jordan: On the client side we suggest an exponential backoff jitter pattern for 5xx and 429. For 429 we also include rate-limit headers so you can back off appropriately. Our SDKs implement a sensible default but we always recommend tuning for your workload.
[02:37] Nadia: From security: we need to know about data retention and encryption at rest. Do you ingest customer prompts for training?
[02:44] Jordan: On hosted we offer options. By default data is retained for X days for troubleshooting but not used for model training. We have an opt-out plus enterprise agreements that ensure no training ingestion. We are SOC2 Type II and offer KMS integrations for dedicated/private. I can share the SOC2 attestation and our security whitepaper.
[03:05] Nadia: KMS integration — is that available on hosted?
[03:08] Jordan: Hosted supports envelope encryption and can integrate with cloud KMS for keys we manage; for full customer-managed keys you typically look at Dedicated or Private that tie to your KMS/HSM. We'll include the matrix in the follow-up.
[03:20] Lisa: Show us a simple code example for chat streaming and relevant params.
[03:25] Sofia: Sure — here's a quick pseudo example: POST /v1/chat with body: model, messages, stream=true, temperature=0.2, max_tokens=150, top_p=0.95, stop=["\n\n"]. Then we open an SSE/chunked response and you receive delta tokens as they generate. If you set stream=false you'll get the whole response.
[03:47] Ravi: How do we control repetition? top_p vs temperature vs presence_penalty?
[03:52] Sofia: temperature controls randomness (lower=more deterministic), top_p is nucleus sampling which controls mass of distribution, presence_penalty discourages repeating tokens seen in context. For many product use cases we lower temperature (0-0.3) and tune top_p, plus use stop sequences to enforce structured output.
[04:10] Mark: Any built-in tools for structured output or tool/function calling?
[04:13] Sofia: We support tool-calling patterns and JSON schema validation helpers. There's a function-calling interface where the model can emit a function call and then you can call your backend. Our console shows examples and you can enable strict JSON mode with schema enforcement.
[04:30] Lisa: On retries for streaming, if we reconnect and the model responds again will we get different text? How do we guarantee user-visible consistency?
[04:38] Sofia: Two parts — idempotency_key for dedupe and resume tokens for partial streams. For final consistency especially with sampling you might still get variation; if determinism is required we recommend lower temperature + deterministic sampling or using a non-sampling mode if the model supports it, or use dedicated capacity pinned to model versions to reduce variability across runs.
[05:00] Mark: Costs — what metrics do you show? Token breakdown?
[05:04] Jordan: Console shows token-level cost, per-route breakdown, and you can export CSV. For hosted pricing we charge per input+output token; dedicated has committed throughput pricing. We'll send a sample pricing sheet.
[05:15] Ravi: Any rate-limiting guidance for heavy QPS? We plan spikes at the top of hour.
[05:20] Sofia: We expose rate-limit headers and recommend smoothing spikes with a small queuing layer or burst capacity. Dedicated allows reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and autoscaling policies. For hosted we have soft burst but recommend committed capacity for sustained high QPS.
[05:34] Lisa: Can we do a pilot with 100 rps?
[05:36] Jordan: Absolutely; we'll define pilot success criteria, expected prompts per minute, and run a short benchmark. Sofia will run a benchmark on your sample prompts as a follow-up.
[05:44] Nadia: Compliance note — audit logs and SSO?
[05:48] Jordan: We have RBAC, SAML SSO integrations, and audit logs in the console. We'll share the compliance pack and docs on data residency.
[05:58] Sofia: Demoing the console now — quick look: model selection, streaming toggle, token breakdown, sample requests, and troubleshooting logs. (screen shares) You can replay requests and see token-level timing.
[06:18] Mark: That replay feature looks helpful for debugging hallucinations.
[06:21] Sofia: Yep, you can replay with same idempotency key and see the trace.
[06:26] Lisa: Any gotchas with webhooks and ephemeral streams?
[06:30] Sofia: Webhooks are for async jobs; for streaming we recommend websockets or SSE to keep low-latency real-time UX. If you need server-to-server callbacks we support webhook fallback with delivery retries.
[06:43] Ravi: Ok curious about model variants — is there automatic fallback to smaller/smarter models on capacity constraints?
[06:49] Jordan: We support routing policies - you can set latency-first or cost-first. If primary model is unavailable we can fallback to compatible variants. We advertise performance profiles per model in the catalog.
[07:00] Lisa: Questions on throttles again — do you provide client-side SDKs that handle backoff and streaming correctly?
[07:05] Sofia: Yes, we have official SDKs (Python, Node) that implement streaming clients, resume, idempotency helpers, and retry/backoff policies. We'll share code snippets in the follow-up.
[07:16] Mark: Anything about model updates and version pinning?
[07:20] Jordan: You can pin to a model version and use rollout policies for canary or A/B. The console has rollout controls.
[07:28] Lisa: Great — let's recap next steps.
[07:32] Jordan: Recap: Jordan to send pricing and security docs (SOC2, SSO matrix); Sofia to run benchmark with your prompt set and share results; Arcadia to confirm pilot scope and provide sample prompts + expected QPS.
[07:48] Mark: That works. We'll aim to get the prompt set over by end of week.
[07:52] Ravi: I'll put together the QPS numbers and sample prompts.
[07:55] Nadia: I'll review the compliance docs once Jordan shares.
[08:00] Jordan: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invite for pilot kickoff.
[08:05] Lisa: Thanks much.
[08:07] Sofia: Thanks, bye.

Notes: small transcription errors present (e.g., KV cache heard as K-V cash in one segment). References: demo slides, pricing sheet, SOC2 report (links to be shared).
